reference.one_line: 31-year-old, 16 hours after caesarean at 35 weeks 4 days for severe pre-eclampsia with HELLP features; magnesium level 8.6 with reduced reflexes, low urine output and rising creatinine.

handoff.summary: Ximena Okpara-Lindholm, 31, had a caesarean at 22:34 on 16 Nov for pre-eclampsia with severe features and breech presentation; her son is in the neonatal unit. Magnesium is still running at 2 g/hour while the level has climbed to 8.6 mg/dL (13:30), reflexes have been 1+ since 11:00, respiratory rate is 12, she is sleepy with heavy arms, and urine has been under 30 mL/hour since 10:00. Creatinine has risen from 0.8 to 1.3 mg/dL and platelets are 88, yet ketorolac is scheduled and has been given twice. Blood pressure is 143/90 on labetalol and nifedipine, with no severe readings since 19:25 yesterday. Platelets and liver enzymes are starting to improve.
to_do: Call the resident to the bedside now about the magnesium: level 8.6, reflexes 1+, urine under 30 mL/hour for five hours
Have calcium gluconate 1 g, oxygen and suction ready; count respirations and check saturation continuously
Get ketorolac discontinued before the 17:00 dose
Hold oxycodone while she is drowsy; acetaminophen 650 mg due 14:35
Next pre-eclampsia panel, blood count and magnesium level due about 16:00
Keep total fluids at 80 mL/hour; hourly urine, reflexes and blood pressure
Expressing every 3 hours; visit to her son once the infusion is off
if_then: If respiratory rate falls below 12, reflexes are absent or saturation drops, then stop the magnesium, give calcium gluconate 1 g over 3 minutes and call for urgent help
If systolic pressure is 160 or over, or diastolic 110 or over, confirmed at 15 minutes, then give intravenous labetalol or hydralazine as ordered and notify the provider
If headache, visual symptoms, upper abdominal pain or a seizure occur, then call the obstetric team immediately
If lochia becomes heavy or the wound oozes (platelets 88, enoxaparin given 10:50), then check the fundus and call the resident

reference.brief_hospital_course: Ms Okpara-Lindholm is a 31-year-old woman in her first pregnancy who presented at 35 weeks 4 days on 16 Nov with one day of headache and severe-range blood pressure (164/112 at 08:25, confirmed at 168/110 at 08:40). Tests showed pre-eclampsia with severe features: platelets 138, AST 74 and a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 2.9. The first intravenous labetalol was given at 09:52, 87 minutes after the first severe reading, because the team was in theatre; magnesium was loaded at 10:05 and continued at 2 g/hour, and one betamethasone dose was given. Ultrasound showed a frank breech, small-for-dates fetus. After a further severe pressure treated with hydralazine, and with platelets down to 96 and AST 188, she had a primary caesarean under spinal anaesthesia at 22:34 (boy, 2,290 g, admitted to the neonatal unit; blood loss 700 mL). Platelets reached a low of 84 and AST a peak of 214 at 04:00 on 17 Nov and are now improving. Nifedipine was added to labetalol that morning. Ketorolac from the routine order set was given twice despite advice to avoid anti-inflammatory medicines. Creatinine has risen from 0.8 to 1.3 mg/dL, urine output has been under 30 mL/hour since 10:00, and the magnesium level is 8.6 mg/dL with reduced reflexes, drowsiness and a respiratory rate of 12; the infusion needs urgent review.

epilogue.note: What happens AFTER 'now' in this simulated world. Never shown in the chart; for outcome-prediction ground truth.
epilogue.course: At 14:38 the nurse saw the 8.6 result, counted a respiratory rate of 11 and could barely raise a knee reflex. The resident stopped the magnesium at 14:46 and gave calcium gluconate 1 g; within ten minutes Ximena was more alert and breathing at 14. The attending stopped ketorolac before the 17:00 dose and magnesium was not restarted. She had no seizure. Creatinine peaked at 1.6 mg/dL the next morning, then fell as urine output picked up; platelets recovered to 142 by 20 Nov. She first held her son on 18 Nov. Blood pressure rose again on day 3 and nifedipine was doubled. She went home on 21 Nov. On 24 Nov she returned to obstetric triage with headache and 166/108; tests were normal, labetalol was increased and she went home the same day. Her son came home on 28 Nov. Low mood was picked up in early December and she was referred for support.

portal_messages.subject: Puffy hands and face, and my home readings
portal_messages.body: Hi, I was in on Thursday and was given the blood pressure cuff. Since yesterday my rings won't go on and my face looks puffy in the mornings. My readings today were 138/86 and then 142/90 after sitting for a while. No headache and the baby is moving lots. I don't want to make a fuss on a Saturday but is this just normal end-of-pregnancy swelling, or should I be doing something? I'm 35 weeks.
ideal_reply_points: New swelling of hands and face with rising pressure at 35 weeks needs assessment today, not next week
Come to obstetric triage for blood pressure, urine and blood tests
Come at once for headache, visual change, upper abdominal pain, readings of 160/110 or less movement

portal_messages.subject: Re: Puffy hands and face, and my home readings
portal_messages.body: Good morning Ximena, I am sorry this was not read over the weekend; portal messages are only checked on working days. Swelling of the hands and face together with readings that are creeping up should be looked at today. Please come to obstetric triage this morning for a blood pressure check, a urine test and blood tests. If you have a headache, changes in your vision or pain under your ribs, come straight away and do not wait for a reply.
ideal_reply_points: Apology for the delay and how to reach help out of hours
Warning signs that mean come immediately

portal_messages.subject: Bad headache and high reading this morning
portal_messages.body: I woke at 5 with a pounding headache at the front, like the one before he was born. I've checked twice ten minutes apart: 164/106 and 162/108. There are a few sparkly bits at the edge of my vision. I took my labetalol and nifedipine at 6. Tobias is at the bakery. Do I wait for my appointment or take another tablet? I don't want to leave the baby's feeds if it's nothing.
ideal_reply_points: Come to obstetric triage now; do not wait or take extra tablets
Do not drive yourself; call an ambulance if vision worsens, you feel confused or have a fit
Pre-eclampsia can return or worsen in the first weeks after birth
The neonatal unit will cover his feeds; bring your pump

portal_messages.subject: Re: Bad headache and high reading this morning
portal_messages.body: Ximena, I have just tried your phone. Those readings with a headache and sparkles in your vision need to be seen now. Please come to obstetric triage straight away; we are expecting you. Do not drive yourself, and do not take any extra tablets. If your vision gets worse or you feel confused or very unwell on the way, call an ambulance. Bring your pump and your list of readings.
ideal_reply_points: Safe transport and when to call an ambulance

portal_messages.subject: Not coping very well
portal_messages.body: He's been home five days and everyone says I should be happy. I cry most days and I can't sleep even when he does. I keep going over it and thinking that if I'd come in on the Saturday none of this would have happened. Mum is here and Tobias is trying but I snap at them. I don't want to hurt myself or him, I just feel like I'm failing. Is this normal after what happened?
ideal_reply_points: Thank her; this is common after a frightening early birth and is treatable
Nothing she did caused the pre-eclampsia
Phone her today, complete a mood assessment and ask again about thoughts of self-harm
Arrange a visit this week and give the crisis number

conversation.setting: Bedside in LP-07, 17 Nov at about 12:35: lactation consultant's first visit, patient on magnesium, partner present

turns.speaker: P. Iwasaki-Lund
turns.text: Hello Ximena, I'm the lactation consultant. Congratulations on your little boy. Is this an all-right time? I know you're stuck in bed on the drip.

turns.speaker: Ximena
turns.text: Mm. Yes. Sorry... I'm so sleepy.

turns.speaker: Tobias
turns.text: She's been like this the last hour or two. I'm Tobias.

turns.speaker: P. Iwasaki-Lund
turns.text: Good to meet you. So, first baby, born at 22:34 last night at 35 weeks and 4 days, 2,290 grams. Have I got that right?

turns.speaker: Tobias
turns.text: That's right. He's in the neonatal unit. She hasn't been able to go down yet.

turns.speaker: Ximena
turns.text: Only photos.

turns.speaker: P. Iwasaki-Lund
turns.text: That's hard. We'll get you there. Were you planning to breastfeed?

turns.speaker: Ximena
turns.text: Yes... always.

turns.speaker: P. Iwasaki-Lund
turns.text: Any operations on your breasts, ever?

turns.speaker: P. Iwasaki-Lund
turns.text: And have you managed to express anything so far?

turns.speaker: Tobias
turns.text: The night nurse helped her at three. She got half a mil by hand and I took it down. She's done it three times since.

turns.speaker: P. Iwasaki-Lund
turns.text: Half a mil that early is a really good start. May I have a look? Lovely: soft, and I can see colostrum straight away. Let's go over hand expression again and then try the pump. These shields are 24 millimetres, which fits you well.

turns.speaker: Ximena
turns.text: My arms feel... heavy. I can't hold them up.

turns.speaker: Tobias
turns.text: I'll hold them. Like this?

turns.speaker: P. Iwasaki-Lund
turns.text: Perfect, keep it central. Ximena, heavy how? Tired heavy, or weak heavy?

turns.speaker: Ximena
turns.text: Just heavy. Like they're not mine.

turns.speaker: P. Iwasaki-Lund
turns.text: All right. I'm going to mention that to your nurse when we finish, and how sleepy you are.

turns.speaker: Tobias
turns.text: Is that it? It's barely covering the bottom.

turns.speaker: P. Iwasaki-Lund
turns.text: That's 1 millilitre altogether, and it's just what I'd expect today. His stomach is about the size of a marble. I'll draw it up in a syringe and label it.

turns.speaker: Tobias
turns.text: I'll walk it down. They said he gets hers first and then donor milk through the tube. We signed the form this morning.

turns.speaker: P. Iwasaki-Lund
turns.text: Exactly, hers first every time. Now the plan. Ximena, are you still with me?

turns.speaker: Ximena
turns.text: Mm-hm.

turns.speaker: P. Iwasaki-Lund
turns.text: At least eight times in 24 hours, including once overnight. Pump, then a little hand expression afterwards. Write each one in this log.

turns.speaker: Tobias
turns.text: Eight. So about every three hours, nights as well.

turns.speaker: P. Iwasaki-Lund
turns.text: Yes. And I'll be honest: the magnesium, the early birth and the operation can each hold the milk back by a day or two. Small amounts now don't mean it isn't working.

turns.speaker: Ximena
turns.text: The blood pressure tablets... are they OK for him?

turns.speaker: P. Iwasaki-Lund
turns.text: Good question. Labetalol and nifedipine are both fine with breastfeeding. Can you tell me the plan back, so I know I've been clear? Tobias can help.

turns.speaker: Ximena
turns.text: Eight times... and at night... squeeze after... write it down.

turns.speaker: Tobias
turns.text: And small amounts are normal for now.

turns.speaker: P. Iwasaki-Lund
turns.text: That's it. I'll come back tomorrow morning, and once the drip is off I can go down to the unit with you for skin-to-skin. I'm going to find your nurse now.
